summary: Reviews how roaming systems were designed and built in 1997, where a user of one network provider can dial in through another. Examples include groups of internet providers sharing access and companies letting staff connect from elsewhere. It is an informational survey rather than a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: It is a report on how you can use your internet account from someone else's phone line, like using your own bank card at another bank's cash machine.

questions: how do isp roaming agreements work
how does radius proxy roaming work
what is a realm in radius
subtitle: A 1997 survey of how ISP roaming worked in practice at GRIC, i-Pass, ChinaNet, Microsoft, MichNet and FidoNet.

tldr.problem: Users wanted to dial in through any of several ISPs while keeping an account with only one, but each roaming effort solved phone numbers, authentication and billing in its own way.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes each system against a common checklist: phone number presentation, exchange, compilation and update, connection management, authentication, NAS configuration, addressing, security and accounting. Most systems route a user@domain login to the home ISP, usually over RADIUS.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational survey, not a specification. It records how six implementations worked in 1997 and points out the pain points, such as conflicting RADIUS attributes.

today: RFC 2194 is an Informational survey with no recorded replacement or update. It describes systems as they stood in September 1997, so its product details should be read as history. The RADIUS protocol it relies on is described in RFC 2058.

sections.title: What Roaming Needs
sections.content:
The memo defines roaming loosely as the ability to use any one of multiple ISPs while keeping a formal customer-vendor relationship with only one. Examples are ISP confederations and ISP-provided corporate network access, possibly with a Virtual Private Network over tunneling protocols such as PPTP, L2F or L2TP.

It lists a first-cut set of requirements and then reviews each implementation against it: phone number presentation, phone number exchange, phone book compilation, phone book update, connection management, authentication, NAS configuration and authorization, address assignment and routing, security, and accounting.

Key terms: the home ISP holds the user's account, and the local ISP is the one the user calls. A phone book is a database of dial-up access numbers and attributes. Shared use networks and non-IP dialup networks (FidoNet is an example) are also reviewed because they address several of the same problems.
sections.eli5: To use someone else's phone line for your account, you need to find a number to call, prove who you are, and have someone keep track of who owes whom.

sections.title: Forwarding Logins to the Home ISP
sections.content:
Most of the systems identify a roamer by the login name. At GRIC (Global Reach Internet Connection), users log in with an e-mail style ID such as liu@Aimnet.com. If the ID has an @ and a domain, the AimTraveler Authentication Server asks a routing server for the home ISP's authentication server, then sends the request there. The home server replies with permission granted or a rejection, and the local NAS then assigns a dynamic address or drops the user.

i-Pass uses username@auth_domain. The local ISP forwards such requests to an i-Pass server, which logs them and passes them to the home ISP. The home ISP uses its normal method and returns YES or NO. ChinaNet and Microsoft use RADIUS proxies and the username@realm form. ChinaNet caches successful roaming users for 3 days by default. Microsoft also supports a prefix form such as MSN/aboba, made for NAS devices with small maximum userID lengths, while RADIUS allows 253 octet userIDs.

Microsoft maps domains to RADIUS servers with static configuration files and suggests DNS SRV records as a more scalable approach for larger consortia.
sections.eli5: When you type your name with an at-sign and a company name, the stranger's computer knows which company to call to check your password.

sections.title: Phone Books and NAS Attribute Conflicts
sections.content:
Phone book handling varies. GRIC compiles books manually by concatenating members' numbers, and users get them by a Web directory or a Java phone book client. i-Pass keeps an Access Point Database and offers a Windows Dial Wizard. Microsoft's Connection Manager downloads phone book deltas by an HTTP GET each time the user logs on, applying difference files in which a deletion is an entry with everything zeroed. Digital signatures are required only for downloaded executables. FidoNet distributes a weekly Nodelist of about 35,000 entries as compressed difference files called Nodediffs.

The Microsoft section also explains a RADIUS problem. The local NAS may differ from the home NAS, so the proxy may need to discard or replace attributes such as Framed-IP-Address, Filter-Id, Vendor-Specific, Session-Timeout and Idle-Timeout. Filter IDs are hard to keep aligned and vendor-specific attributes have meaning only to one vendor's devices. RADIUS does not distinguish mandatory from optional attributes, so the proxy cannot tell what is safe to drop.
sections.eli5: Everyone keeps a list of phone numbers and has to keep it up to date. Different machines also speak slightly different dialects, so the middle computer sometimes has to translate.

sections.title: MichNet and Shared Dial-In Policy
sections.content:
MichNet, run by Merit Network, gave each participating organization a realm-name, and users logged in as user@realm. Merit-run RADIUS core servers proxied requests to each realm's own AAA server and enforced a common policy: providers must make spare dial-in ports available to guests. Guests are denied when few ports remain and are limited to a time limit (one hour during prime time, two hours otherwise). Each realm is allocated a number of simultaneous access tokens (SATs) that cap its guests.

For outside services such as a national 800 number, Merit forwards requests to the member's server for approval, logs sessions and bills members monthly. The memo says the core servers see the user password in the clear when they decode and re-encode a request, which is why Merit staff run them. As of May 1, 1997, MichNet reported 11 members, 405 affiliates and 4774 dial-in lines.

The memo also covers the AAA server software Merit developed and the Merit AAA Server Consortium.
sections.eli5: Everyone lends out their spare phone lines, but only a limited number of visitors may use them at once, and they have a time limit.

sections.title: Accounting, Security and FidoNet
sections.content:
Settlement is handled by a central party in most systems: AimQuest for GRIC, i-Pass as clearinghouse, MSN as settlement agent, Merit for MichNet, and a central server of China Telecom for ChinaNet, which bills provincial ISPs monthly. Microsoft transfers compressed accounting records by FTP, started by the receiver, and warns that its default record format is not extensible, which customers saw as a serious limitation.

On security, the memo itself only points to its sections 5.6 and 6.5. GRIC hashes the password with MD5 between its servers. i-Pass encrypts all transactions with SSL and acts as the certificate authority. ChinaNet encrypts between its RADIUS servers. Token cards and tunneling are not supported by GRIC's or Microsoft's servers.

FidoNet is a contrast: it has no distributed authentication or accounting, so users may not roam between systems. The memo notes that coordinator submissions have no security, which leaves open fraudulent updates, and cites a proposal to add a shared secret.
sections.eli5: Someone in the middle adds up who used whose phone lines and sends the bills. FidoNet only shared phone lists, so you could not roam at all.
